shortness-of-life_section-01.originalText:
The greater part of mankind, my Paulinus, complains of the
unkindness of Nature, because we are born only for a short space
of time, and that this allotted period of life runs away so swiftly,
nay so hurriedly, that with but few exceptions men’s life comes to
an end just as they are preparing to enjoy it: nor is it only the
common herd and the ignorant vulgar who mourn over this universal
misfortune, as they consider it to be: this reflection has wrung
complaints even from great men. Hence comes that well-known saying
of physicians, that art is long but life is short: hence arose that
quarrel, so unbefitting a sage, which Aristotle picked with Nature,
because she had indulged animals with such length of days that some
of them lived for ten or fifteen centuries, while man, although
born for many and such great exploits, had the term of his existence
cut so much shorter.
shortness-of-life_section-01.plainEnglish: Most people, Paulinus, complain that nature has been unfair to us. They say we are born with too little time, and that even the time we are given slips away far too quickly. In fact, it rushes by so fast that most people's lives end just as they're getting ready to truly live. It's not just ordinary people and the uneducated masses who grieve over what they see as this universal tragedy. Even great thinkers have complained about it. That's where the famous medical saying comes from: "The art is long, but life is short." It's also why Aristotle — hardly fitting for a wise man — picked a fight with Nature herself. He was angry that she gave animals such long lives that some live for ten or fifteen centuries, while humans, born for so many great deeds, get their time cut painfully short.

shortness-of-life_section-01.originalText:
We do not have a very short time assigned to
us, but we lose a great deal of it: life is long enough to carry
out the most important projects: we have an ample portion,
if we do but arrange the whole of it aright: but when it all runs
to waste through luxury and carelessness, when it is not devoted
to any good purpose, then at the last we are forced to feel that
it is all over, although we never noticed how it glided away. Thus
it is: we do not receive a short life, but we make it a short one,
and we are not poor in days, but wasteful of them. When great and
kinglike riches fall into the hands of a bad master, they are
dispersed straightway, but even a moderate fortune, when bestowed
upon a wise guardian, increases by use: and in like manner our life
has great opportunities for one who knows how to dispose of it to
the best advantage.
shortness-of-life_section-01.plainEnglish: We haven't been given a short life. We've just wasted a lot of it. Life is long enough to do great things — if you stop throwing it away. We have plenty of time, but only if we use it wisely. When we waste our days on luxury and carelessness, when we don't put our time toward anything worthwhile, then suddenly we realize it's all gone. We never even noticed it slipping away. That's the truth: we don't get a short life, we make it short. We're not poor in days — we're just wasteful with them. When great wealth falls into the hands of a fool, it vanishes quickly. But even a modest fortune grows when a wise person manages it. Our life works the same way. It offers great opportunities to anyone who knows how to use it well.

shortness-of-life_section-02.originalText:
Why do we complain of Nature? she has dealt kindly with us. Life is long enough, if you know how to use it. One man is possessed by an avarice which nothing can satisfy, another by a laborious diligence in doing what is totally useless: another is sodden by wine: another is benumbed by sloth: one man is exhausted by an ambition which makes him court the good will of others: another, through his eagerness as a merchant, is led to visit every land and every sea by the hope of gain: some are plagued by the love of soldiering, and are always either endangering other men's lives or in trembling for their own: some wear away their lives in that voluntary slavery, the unrequited service of great men: many are occupied either in laying claim to other men's fortune or in complaining of their own: a great number have no settled purpose, and are tossed from one new scheme to another by a rambling, inconsistent, dissatisfied, fickle habit of mind: some care for no object sufficiently to try to attain it, but lie lazily yawning until their fate comes upon them: so that I cannot doubt the truth of that verse which the greatest of poets has dressed in the guise of an oracular response—

"We live a small part only of our lives."
shortness-of-life_section-02.plainEnglish: Why do we blame nature? She has been generous to us. Life is long enough — if you know how to use it. One person is driven by greed that can never be satisfied. Another works frantically at completely pointless tasks. One drowns himself in wine. Another is paralyzed by laziness. One man exhausts himself chasing ambition, constantly seeking other people's approval. Another travels the world as a merchant, chasing profit across every land and sea. Some are obsessed with war, always putting others in danger or fearing for their own lives. Others waste their lives in willing slavery, serving powerful men who never repay their loyalty. Many spend their time either scheming to steal other people's wealth or complaining about their own poverty. A great number have no clear purpose at all. They drift from one whim to another, restless and fickle and never satisfied. Some people care so little about anything that they don't even try. They just lie around yawning until death finds them. So I believe that greatest of poets was right when he wrote: "We live only a small part of our lives."

shortness-of-life_section-02.originalText: But all duration is time, not life: vices press upon us and surround us on every side, and do not permit us to regain our feet, or to raise our eyes and gaze upon truth, but when we are down keep us prostrate and chained to low desires. Men who are in this condition are never allowed to come to themselves: if ever by chance they obtain any rest, they roll to and fro like the deep sea, which heaves and tosses after a gale, and they never have any respite from their lusts. Do you suppose that I speak of those whose ills are notorious? Nay, look at those whose prosperity all men run to see: they are choked by their own good things. To how many men do riches prove a heavy burden? how many men's eloquence and continual desire to display their own cleverness has cost them their lives? how many are sallow with constant sensual indulgence? how many have no freedom left them by the tribe of clients that surges around them?
shortness-of-life_section-02.plainEnglish: But all duration is time, not life. Vices press in on us from every side. They don't let us get back on our feet or lift our eyes to see the truth. When we're down, they keep us flat on the ground, chained to shallow desires. People in this state never get a chance to find themselves again. If they ever get a moment's rest, they roll around like the ocean after a storm — heaving and tossing with no break from their cravings. You think I'm talking about people whose problems are obvious? No, look at those whose success everyone envies. They're choking on their own good fortune. How many people are crushed by their wealth? How many have died because of their eloquence and constant need to show off their cleverness? How many are pale and sick from endless pleasure-seeking? How many have lost all freedom because of the crowd of clients swarming around them?

shortness-of-life_section-02.originalText: Look through all these, from the lowest to the highest:—this man calls his friends to support him, this one is present in court, this one is the defendant, this one pleads for him, this one is on the jury: but no one lays claim to his own self, every one wastes his time over some one else. Investigate those men, whose names are in every one's mouth: you will find that they bear just the same marks: A is devoted to B, and B to C: no one belongs to himself. Moreover some men are full of most irrational anger: they complain of the insolence of their chiefs, because they have not granted them an audience when they wished for it; as if a man had any right to complain of being so haughtily shut out by another, when he never has leisure to give his own conscience a hearing. This chief of yours, whoever he is, though he may look at you in an offensive manner, still will some day look at you, open his ears to your words, and give you a seat by his side: but you never design to look upon yourself, to listen to your own grievances. You ought not, then, to claim these services from another, especially since while you yourself were doing so, you did not wish for an interview with another man, but were not able to obtain one with yourself.
shortness-of-life_section-02.plainEnglish: Look at everyone around you, from bottom to top. This person is calling friends for support. That one is in court. Another is the defendant. Someone else is arguing the case. Another sits on the jury. But no one claims ownership of their own life. Everyone wastes their time on someone else. Look at the famous people whose names everyone knows. You'll see the same pattern. Person A devotes himself to Person B. Person B devotes himself to Person C. No one belongs to himself. Some people get irrationally angry about this. They complain that their bosses are arrogant for not granting them a meeting when they wanted one. As if they have any right to complain about being shut out by someone else when they never make time to listen to their own conscience! Your boss, whoever he is, might look at you rudely now. But someday he will look at you, listen to your words, and give you a seat beside him. But you never bother to look at yourself or listen to your own complaints. So you shouldn't demand these services from someone else. Especially since while you were trying to get that meeting, you didn't want an interview with another person — you just couldn't manage to get one with yourself.

shortness-of-life_section-03.originalText: Were all the brightest intellects of all time to employ themselves on this one subject, they never could sufficiently express their wonder at this blindness of men's minds: men will not allow any one to establish himself upon their estates, and upon the most trifling dispute about the measuring of boundaries, they betake themselves to stones and cudgels: yet they allow others to encroach upon their lives, nay, they themselves actually lead others in to take possession of them. You cannot find any one who wants to distribute his money; yet among how many people does every one distribute his life? men covetously guard their property from waste, but when it comes to waste of time, they are most prodigal of that of which it would become them to be sparing.
shortness-of-life_section-03.plainEnglish: Even if all the greatest minds in history worked together on this problem, they could never fully express their amazement at how blind people are. Men won't let anyone set foot on their property. They'll grab stones and clubs over the smallest boundary dispute. Yet they let others invade their lives. In fact, they actually invite people in to take over their time. You can't find anyone willing to give away their money. But everyone gives away their life to countless people. Men jealously guard their wealth from waste. But when it comes to wasting time, they throw away the very thing they should treasure most.

shortness-of-life_section-03.originalText: Let us take one of the elders, and say to him, "We perceive that you have arrived at the extreme limits of human life: you are in your hundredth year, or even older. Come now, reckon up your whole life in black and white: tell us how much of your time has been spent upon your creditors, how much on your mistress, how much on your king, how much on your clients, how much in quarrelling with your wife, how much in keeping your slaves in order, how much in running up and down the city on business. Add to this the diseases which we bring upon us with our own hands, and the time which has laid idle without any use having been made of it; you will see that you have not lived as many years as you count. Look back in your memory and see how often you have been consistent in your projects, how many days passed as you intended them to do when you were at your own disposal, how often you did not change colour and your spirit did not quail, how much work you have done in so long a time, how many people have without your knowledge stolen parts of your life from you, how much you have lost, how large a part has been taken up by useless grief, foolish gladness, greedy desire, or polite conversation; how little of yourself is left to you: you will then perceive that you will die prematurely."
shortness-of-life_section-03.plainEnglish: Let's pick one of the old folks and say to him, "We see you've reached the very edge of human life. You're a hundred years old, maybe more. Now sit down and add up your whole life. Tell us how much time you spent dealing with people you owed money to. How much on your lover. How much serving your king. How much on your clients. How much fighting with your wife. How much keeping your slaves in line. How much running around the city on business. Add in the sicknesses you brought on yourself and all the time you just wasted doing nothing useful. You'll see that you haven't really lived as many years as you think you have. Look back and remember: how often did you stick to your plans? How many days went exactly as you wanted when you were free to choose? How often did you not go pale with fear or lose your nerve? What did you actually accomplish in all that time? How many people stole pieces of your life without you even noticing? How much did you lose? How much got eaten up by pointless grief, silly happiness, greedy wanting, or small talk? How little of yourself is actually left? Then you'll realize that you're dying too soon."

shortness-of-life_section-03.originalText: What, then, is the reason of this? It is that people live as though they would live for ever: you never remember your human frailty; you never notice how much of your time has already gone by: you spend it as though you had an abundant and overflowing store of it, though all the while that day which you devote to some man or to some thing is perhaps your last. You fear everything, like mortals as you are, and yet you desire everything as if you were immortals.
shortness-of-life_section-03.plainEnglish: So what's the problem? People live as if they'll never die. You forget how fragile you are. You don't notice how much time has already slipped away. You spend time carelessly, as if you have an endless supply of it. But that day you waste on someone or something might be your last. You fear everything like the mortal you are, but you want everything like you're going to live forever.

shortness-of-life_section-03.originalText: You will hear many men say, "After my fiftieth year I will give myself up to leisure: my sixtieth shall be my last year of public office": and what guarantee have you that your life will last any longer? who will let all this go on just as you have arranged it? are you not ashamed to reserve only the leavings of your life for yourself, and appoint for the enjoyment of your own right mind only that time which you cannot devote to any business? How late it is to begin life just when we have to be leaving it! What a foolish forgetfulness of our mortality, to put off wholesome counsels until our fiftieth or sixtieth year, and to choose that our lives shall begin at a point which few of us ever reach.
shortness-of-life_section-03.plainEnglish: You'll hear many men say, "After I turn fifty, I'll finally take time for myself. When I'm sixty, I'll quit my public duties." But what guarantee do you have that you'll live that long? Who says life will go according to your neat little plan? Aren't you ashamed to save only the scraps of your life for yourself? You're planning to enjoy your own mind only when you're too old to do anything else. How ridiculous to start living just when you have to die! What foolish forgetfulness of death — putting off wise choices until fifty or sixty, deciding your real life should begin at an age most people never even reach.

shortness-of-life_section-04.originalText: You will find that the most powerful and highly-placed men let fall phrases in which they long for leisure, praise it, and prefer it to all the blessings which they enjoy. Sometimes they would fain descend from their lofty pedestal, if it could be safely done: for Fortune collapses by its own weight, without any shock or interference from without.
shortness-of-life_section-04.plainEnglish: You'll notice that the most powerful and high-ranking people often say they wish they had more free time. They praise leisure and say they'd rather have that than all their wealth and status. Sometimes they'd love to step down from their high positions — if only they could do it safely. But fortune has a way of collapsing under its own weight, even without any outside push.

shortness-of-life_section-04.originalText: The late Emperor Augustus, upon whom the gods bestowed more blessings than on any one else, never ceased to pray for rest and exemption from the troubles of empire: he used to enliven his labours with this sweet, though unreal consolation, that he would some day live for himself alone. In a letter which he addressed to the Senate, after promising that his rest shall not be devoid of dignity nor discreditable to his former glories, I find the following words:—"These things, however, it is more honourable to do than to promise: but my eagerness for that time, so earnestly longed for, has led me to derive a certain pleasure from speaking about it, though the reality is still far distant." He thought leisure so important, that though he could not actually enjoy it, yet he did so by anticipation and by thinking about it.
shortness-of-life_section-04.plainEnglish: Even the late Emperor Augustus — who received more blessings from the gods than anyone — never stopped praying for rest and freedom from the burdens of ruling. He would comfort himself during his hard work with this sweet but imaginary hope: that someday he would live just for himself. In a letter to the Senate, after promising that his retirement would still be dignified and wouldn't shame his past achievements, he wrote: "Of course, it's better to actually do these things than just promise them. But I'm so eager for that time I long for that I get pleasure just from talking about it, even though it's still far away." He thought free time was so valuable that even though he couldn't actually have it, he enjoyed it just by thinking about it.

shortness-of-life_section-04.originalText: He, who saw everything depending upon himself alone, who swayed the fortunes of men and of nations, thought that his happiest day would be that on which he laid aside his greatness. He knew by experience how much labour was involved in that glory that shone through all lands, and how much secret anxiety was concealed within it: he had been forced to assert his rights by war, first with his countrymen, next with his colleagues, and lastly with his own relations, and had shed blood both by sea and by land: after marching his troops under arms through Macedonia, Sicily, Egypt, Syria, Asia Minor, and almost all the countries of the world, when they were weary with slaughtering Romans he had directed them against a foreign foe.
shortness-of-life_section-04.plainEnglish: This man held everything in his hands. He controlled the fate of individuals and entire nations. Yet he believed his happiest day would be the one when he gave up all that power. He learned firsthand how much work it took to maintain that glory that reached every corner of the world. He knew how much hidden worry came with it. He had been forced to fight wars to protect his position — first against his own countrymen, then against his political allies, and finally against his own family. He had spilled blood on both sea and land. He had marched his armies through Macedonia, Sicily, Egypt, Syria, Asia Minor, and nearly every country in the world. When his troops grew tired of killing Romans, he turned them against foreign enemies.

shortness-of-life_section-04.originalText: While he was pacifying the Alpine regions, and subduing the enemies whom he found in the midst of the Roman empire, while he was extending its boundaries beyond the Rhine, the Euphrates, and the Danube, at Rome itself the swords of Murena, Caepio, Lepidus, Egnatius, and others were being sharpened to slay him. Scarcely had he escaped from their plot, when his already failing age was terrified by his daughter and all the noble youths who were pledged to her cause by adultery with her by way of oath of fidelity. Then there was Paulus and Antonius's mistress, a second time to be feared by Rome: and when he had cut out these ulcers from his very limbs, others grew in their place: the empire, like a body overloaded with blood, was always breaking out somewhere. For this reason he longed for leisure: all his labours were based upon hopes and thoughts of leisure: this was the wish of him who could accomplish the wishes of all other men.
shortness-of-life_section-04.plainEnglish: While Augustus was conquering the Alpine regions and defeating enemies within the Roman empire, while he was pushing the borders beyond the Rhine, Euphrates, and Danube rivers, back in Rome itself conspirators like Murena, Caepio, Lepidus, Egnatius, and others were sharpening their swords to kill him. He barely escaped their plot when his failing health was shaken by his own daughter and all the young nobles who had sworn loyalty to her through adultery. Then came the threat of Paulus and Antony's mistress — a second danger to Rome. When he cut out these cancers from his own body, new ones grew in their place. The empire was like a body with too much blood — it kept bursting somewhere. This is why he longed for rest. All his work was driven by the hope of someday having leisure. This was the one wish of a man who could grant everyone else's wishes.

shortness-of-life_section-05.originalText:
While tossed hither and thither by Catiline and Clodius, Pompeius
and Crassus, by some open enemies and some doubtful friends, while
he struggled with the struggling republic and kept it from going
to ruin, when at last he was banished, being neither able to keep
silence in prosperity nor to endure adversity with patience, how
often must Marcus Cicero have cursed that consulship of his which
he never ceased to praise, and which nevertheless deserved it? What
piteous expressions he uses in a letter to Atticus when Pompeius
the father had been defeated, and his son was recruiting his shattered
forces in Spain? “Do you ask,” writes he, “what I am doing here? I
am living in my Tusculan villa almost as a prisoner.” He adds more
afterwards, wherein he laments his former life, complains of the
present, and despairs of the future. Cicero called himself “half a
prisoner,” but, by Hercules, the wise man never would have come
under so lowly a title: he never would be half a prisoner, but would
always enjoy complete and entire liberty, being free, in his own
power, and greater than all others: for what can be greater than
the man who is greater than Fortune?
shortness-of-life_section-05.plainEnglish: Consider Cicero. He was tossed around by Catiline and Clodius, Pompeius and Crassus — some open enemies, some unreliable friends. He fought to save the struggling republic from collapse. Then he was banished. He couldn't stay quiet when things went well, and he couldn't handle adversity with grace. How often must Marcus Cicero have regretted that consulship he never stopped bragging about — even though he deserved the praise? Look at the pitiful things he wrote to Atticus after Pompeius the father was defeated and his son was trying to rebuild his broken forces in Spain. "You ask what I'm doing here?" he writes. "I'm living in my villa at Tusculum, practically a prisoner." He goes on to lament his past life, complain about the present, and despair about the future. Cicero called himself "half a prisoner." But by God, a wise man would never accept such a degrading title. He would never be half a prisoner. He would always enjoy complete and total freedom — free, in control of himself, and greater than everyone else. For what can be greater than the man who is greater than Fortune?

shortness-of-life_section-06.originalText: When Livius Drusus, a vigorous and energetic man, brought forward bills for new laws and radical measures of the Gracchus pattern, being the centre of a vast mob of all the peoples of Italy, and seeing no way to solve the question, since he was not allowed to deal with it as he wished, and yet was not free to throw it up after having once taken part in it, complained bitterly of his life, which had been one of unrest from the very cradle, and said, we are told, that "he was the only person who had never had any holidays even when he was a boy." Indeed, while he was still under age and wearing the praetexta, he had the courage to plead the cause of accused persons in court, and to make use of his influence so powerfully that it is well known that in some causes his exertions gained a verdict. Where would such precocious ambition stop? You may be sure that one who showed such boldness as a child would end by becoming a great pest both in public and in private life: it was too late for him to complain that he had had no holidays, when from his boyhood he had been a firebrand and a nuisance in the courts. It is a stock question whether he committed suicide: for he fell by a sudden wound in the groin, and some doubted whether his death was caused by his own hand, though none disputed its having happened most seasonably.
shortness-of-life_section-06.plainEnglish: Take Livius Drusus — a forceful, energetic man who pushed for new laws and radical reforms like the Gracchus brothers had done. He found himself at the center of huge crowds from all over Italy. But he couldn't see any way out of the mess he'd created. He wasn't allowed to handle things the way he wanted, but he also couldn't just walk away after getting so deeply involved. So he complained bitterly about his life, saying it had been nothing but chaos from the moment he was born. According to the stories, he said "I'm the only person who never had a single holiday, not even as a child." And it was true — even as a young boy still wearing his child's toga, he was bold enough to defend people in court and use his influence so powerfully that everyone knew his efforts had won several cases. Where was that kind of early ambition going to lead? You can be sure that someone who showed such aggression as a child would end up becoming a major problem in both public and private life. It was too late for him to complain about never having holidays when he'd been stirring up trouble in the courts since he was a boy. People still debate whether he killed himself. He died from a sudden wound to his groin, and some questioned whether it was suicide, though everyone agreed the timing was awfully convenient.

shortness-of-life_section-06.originalText: It would be superfluous to mention more who, while others thought them the happiest of men, have themselves borne true witness to their own feelings, and have loathed all that they have done for all the years of their lives: yet by these complaints they have effected no alteration either in others or in themselves: for after these words have escaped them their feelings revert to their accustomed frame. By Hercules, that life of you great men, even though it should last for more than a thousand years, is still a very short one: those vices of yours would swallow up any extent of time: no wonder if this our ordinary span, which, though Nature hurries on, can be enlarged by common sense, soon slips away from you; for you do not lay hold of it or hold it back, and try to delay the swiftest of all things, but you let it pass as though it were a useless thing and you could supply its place.
shortness-of-life_section-06.plainEnglish: I could list many more examples of people who seemed blessed to everyone else, yet confessed their true feelings. They hated everything they had done throughout their entire lives. But these complaints changed nothing — not in others, not in themselves. After speaking these words, their feelings went right back to the old patterns. By God, even if you powerful men lived for a thousand years, your lives would still be short. Your vices would devour any amount of time you were given. No wonder our normal lifespan — which could be stretched longer through wisdom, even though nature rushes it along — slips away from you so quickly. You don't grab hold of it or try to hold it back. You don't try to slow down the fastest thing in the world. Instead, you let it pass by as if it were worthless and you could easily replace it.

shortness-of-life_section-07.originalText: Among these I reckon in the first place those who devote their time to nothing but drinking and debauchery: for no men are busied more shamefully: the others, although the glory which they pursue is but a counterfeit, still deserve some credit for their pursuit of it—though you may tell me of misers, of passionate men, of men who hate and who even wage war without a cause—yet all such men sin like men: but the sin of those who are given up to gluttony and lust is a disgraceful one. Examine all the hours of their lives: consider how much time they spend in calculation, how much in plotting, how much in fear, how much in giving and deceiving flattery, how much in entering into recognizances for themselves or for others, how much in banquets, which indeed become a serious business, you will see that they are not allowed any breathing time either by their pleasures or their pains.
shortness-of-life_section-07.plainEnglish: First on my list are people who spend their time drinking and indulging themselves. No one wastes time more shamefully than they do. At least other people — even the greedy, the angry, those who hate for no reason or start pointless wars — are chasing something that looks like glory. You can criticize them, but they're still pursuing something that seems important to them. They sin, but they sin like human beings. But people who live only for food and pleasure? That's just disgraceful. Look at how these gluttons and pleasure-seekers spend their hours. How much time do they spend scheming? How much worrying? How much giving fake compliments or receiving them? How much time signing contracts and making deals? How much at dinner parties that become serious business themselves? You'll see they get no rest from either their pleasures or their troubles.

shortness-of-life_section-07.originalText: Finally, all are agreed that nothing, neither eloquence nor literature, can be done properly by one who is occupied with something else; for nothing can take deep root in a mind which is directed to some other subject, and which rejects whatever you try to stuff into it. No man knows less about living than a business man: there is nothing about which it is more difficult to gain knowledge. Other arts have many folk everywhere who profess to teach them: some of them can be so thoroughly learned by mere boys, that they are able to teach them to others: but one's whole life must be spent in learning how to live, and, which may perhaps surprise you more, one's whole life must be spent in learning how to die.
shortness-of-life_section-07.plainEnglish: Everyone agrees on this: you can't do anything well — whether speaking or writing — if your mind is busy with other things. Nothing takes deep root in a mind that's constantly distracted and pushes away whatever you try to put into it. No one knows less about living than a businessman. There's nothing harder to learn than how to live. You can find teachers for other skills everywhere. Some skills are so simple that children can master them and then teach others. But learning how to live takes your entire lifetime. And what might surprise you even more — learning how to die also takes your entire lifetime.

shortness-of-life_section-07.originalText: Many excellent men have freed themselves from all hindrances, have given up riches, business, and pleasure, and have made it their duty to the very end of their lives to learn how to live: and yet the larger portion of them leave this life confessing that they do not yet know how to live, and still less know how to live as wise men. Believe me, it requires a great man and one who is superior to human frailties not to allow any of his time to be filched from him: and therefore it follows that his life is a very long one, because he devotes every possible part of it to himself: no portion lies idle or uncultivated, or in another man's power; for he finds nothing worthy of being exchanged for his time, which he husbands most grudgingly. He, therefore, had time enough: whereas those who gave up a great part of their lives to the people of necessity had not enough.
shortness-of-life_section-07.plainEnglish:
Many excellent people have freed themselves from all distractions. They've given up wealth, business deals, and pleasures. They've made it their life's work to learn how to live well. Yet most of them die admitting they still don't know how to live — let alone how to live wisely.

Believe me, it takes a great person to protect their time from being stolen. Someone who rises above human weaknesses won't let anyone take even a minute from them. That's why their life feels very long — they give every possible moment to themselves. No part of their time sits idle or wasted or under someone else's control. They find nothing worth trading their time for, and they guard it fiercely.

Such a person has enough time. But those who give most of their lives to other people will always run short.

shortness-of-life_section-07.originalText: Yet you need not suppose that the latter were not sometimes conscious of their loss: indeed, you will hear most of those who are troubled with great prosperity every now and then cry out amid their hosts of clients, their pleadings in court, and their other honourable troubles, "I am not allowed to live my own life." Why is he not allowed? because all those who call upon you to defend them, take you away from yourself. How many of your days have been spent by that defendant? by that candidate for office? by that old woman who is weary with burying her heirs? by that man who pretends to be ill, in order to excite the greed of those who hope to inherit his property? by that powerful friend of yours, who uses you to swell his train, not to be his friend? Balance your account, and run over all the days of your life; you will see that only a very few days, and only those which were useless for any other purpose, have been left to you.
shortness-of-life_section-07.plainEnglish: But don't think wealthy people are unaware of what they're losing. You'll often hear those blessed with great success cry out, even surrounded by their crowds of followers and important legal cases: "I can't live my own life!" Why can't he? Because everyone who calls on him for help steals him away from himself. How many days have you lost to that client you're defending? To that person running for office? To that old woman tired of outliving her heirs? To that man faking illness to make his potential inheritors more eager? To that powerful friend who uses you as decoration in his entourage, not as a real friend? Add it all up. Go through every day of your life. You'll find that only a handful of days — the ones too worthless for anyone else to claim — were actually yours.

shortness-of-life_section-07.originalText: He who has obtained the _fasces_[6] for which he longed, is eager to get rid of them, and is constantly saying, "When will this year be over?" another exhibits public games, and once would have given a great deal for the chance of doing so, but now "when," says he, "shall I escape from this?" another is an advocate who is fought for in all the courts, and who draws immense audiences, who crowd all the forum to a far greater distance than they can hear him; "When," says he, "will vacation-time come?" Every man hurries through his life, and suffers from a yearning for the future, and a weariness of the present: but he who disposes of all his time for his own purposes, who arranges all his days as though he were arranging the plan of his life, neither wishes for nor fears the morrow: for what new pleasure can any hour now bestow upon him? he knows it all, and has indulged in it all even to satiety.
shortness-of-life_section-07.plainEnglish: The person who gets the political office he desperately wanted now can't wait to get rid of it. He keeps saying, "When will this year be over?" Another person puts on expensive public games — something he once would have paid dearly for the chance to do. Now he asks, "When can I escape from this?" Another is a famous lawyer who packs the courtrooms. Crowds fill the entire forum, stretching far beyond where they can even hear him speak. But he asks, "When will vacation time come?" Everyone rushes through life. They long for the future and feel tired of the present. But the person who uses all his time for his own purposes — who plans each day as if he's planning his whole life — doesn't wish for tomorrow or fear it. What new pleasure could any hour bring him? He knows it all. He's experienced it all, even to the point of being sick of it.

shortness-of-life_section-07.originalText: Fortune may deal with the rest as she will, his life is already safe from her: such a man may gain something, but cannot lose anything: and, indeed, he can only gain anything in the same way as one who is already glutted and filled can get some extra food which he takes although he does not want it. You have no grounds, therefore, for supposing that any one has lived long, because he has wrinkles or grey hairs: such a man has not lived long, but has only been long alive. Why! would you think that a man had voyaged much if a fierce gale had caught him as soon as he left his port, and he had been driven round and round the same place continually by a succession of winds blowing from opposite quarters? such a man has not travelled much, he has only been much tossed about.
shortness-of-life_section-07.plainEnglish: Fortune can do what she wants with everything else — this man's life is already protected from her. He might gain something, but he can't lose anything. He can only gain things the way someone who's already stuffed with food might take another bite even though he doesn't want it. So don't assume someone has lived a long life just because he has wrinkles or gray hair. That person hasn't lived long — he's just been alive for a long time. Think about it this way: would you say a sailor had traveled far if a storm caught him right after leaving port and kept spinning him in circles with winds blowing from every direction? That sailor didn't travel much. He just got tossed around a lot.

shortness-of-life_section-08.originalText: I am filled with wonder when I see some men asking others for their time, and those who are asked for it most willing to give it: both parties consider the object for which the time is given, but neither of them thinks of the time itself, as though in asking for this one asked for nothing, and in giving it one gave nothing: we play with what is the most precious of all things: yet it escapes men's notice, because it is an incorporeal thing, and because it does not come before our eyes; and therefore it is held very cheap, nay, hardly any value whatever is put upon it. Men set the greatest store upon presents or pensions, and hire out their work, their services, or their care in order to gain them: no one values time: they give it much more freely, as though it cost nothing.
shortness-of-life_section-08.plainEnglish: I'm amazed when I see people asking others for their time, and those others being so willing to give it. Both people think about what the time will be used for. But neither thinks about the time itself. It's as if asking for time costs nothing and giving it away costs nothing. We treat the most precious thing in the world like a game. People don't notice this because time has no physical form. You can't see it or touch it. So we think it's worthless — or close to worthless. People treasure gifts and money. They work hard to earn these things. But no one values time. We give it away freely, as if it costs us nothing.

shortness-of-life_section-08.originalText: Yet you will see these same people clasping the knees of their physician as suppliants when they are sick and in present peril of death, and if threatened with a capital charge willing to give all that they possess in order that they may live: so inconsistent are they. Indeed, if the number of every man's future years could be laid before him, as we can lay that of his past years, how anxious those who found that they had but few years remaining would be to make the most of them? Yet it is easy to arrange the distribution of a quantity, however small, if we know how much there is: what you ought to husband most carefully is that which may run short you know not when.
shortness-of-life_section-08.plainEnglish: Yet you will see these same people begging their doctors to save them when they're sick and facing death. If they're charged with a crime that could kill them, they'll give away everything they own just to stay alive. How inconsistent they are! If we could see how many years we have left — the way we can count the years already behind us — those with only a few years remaining would panic. They'd desperately try to make the most of their time. It's easy to manage any amount of something when you know exactly how much you have. But the thing you should guard most carefully is the thing that might run out at any moment — and you have no idea when.

shortness-of-life_section-08.originalText: Yet you have no reason to suppose that they do not know how dear a thing time is: they are wont to say to those whom they especially love that they are ready to give them a part of their own years. They do give them, and know not that they are giving them; but they give them in such a manner that they themselves lose them without the others gaining them. They do not, however, know whence they obtain their supply, and therefore they are able to endure the waste of what is not seen: yet no one will give you back your years, no one will restore them to you again: your life will run its course when once it has begun, and will neither begin again or efface what it has done.
shortness-of-life_section-08.plainEnglish: You might think these people don't understand how precious time is. But they do. They tell the people they love most that they'd gladly give them some of their own years. And they do give them away — without realizing it. But they give their time in ways where they lose it and their loved ones don't actually gain anything. They don't understand where their time comes from, so they can stand to waste what they can't see. But here's the thing: no one will give you back your lost years. No one can restore them to you. Once your life starts moving, it won't start over or undo what's already been done.

shortness-of-life_section-08.originalText: It will make no disturbance, it will give you no warning of how fast it flies: it will move silently on: it will not prolong itself at the command of a king, or at the wish of a nation: as it started on its first day, so it will run: it will never turn aside, never delay. What follows, then? Why! you are busy, but life is hurrying on: death will be here some time or other, and you must attend to him, whether you will or no.
shortness-of-life_section-08.plainEnglish: Time won't announce itself or warn you how quickly it's passing. It moves in silence. No king can command it to slow down. No nation can wish for more of it. Time runs at the same pace it started with on day one. It never turns aside. It never delays. So what does this mean? You're busy with your tasks, but life is rushing past you. Death will arrive eventually, and you'll have to face him whether you want to or not.

shortness-of-life_section-09.originalText: Can anything be mentioned which is more insane than the ideas of leisure of those people who boast of their worldly wisdom? They live laboriously, in order that they may live better; they fit themselves out for life at the expense of life itself, and cast their thoughts a long way forwards: yet postponement is the greatest waste of life: it wrings day after day from us, and takes away the present by promising something hereafter: there is no such obstacle to true living as waiting, which loses to-day while it is depending on the morrow. You dispose of that which is in the hand of Fortune, and you let go that which is in your own. Whither are you looking, whither are you stretching forward? everything future is uncertain: live now straightway.
shortness-of-life_section-09.plainEnglish: Is there anything more insane than how so-called wise people think about free time? They work themselves to death trying to build a better life. They prepare for living by sacrificing life itself. They're always planning far into the future. But delay is the biggest thief of life. It steals each day from us. It robs us of the present by promising something better later. Nothing blocks real living like waiting — losing today while depending on tomorrow. You're betting on what Fortune controls, while letting go of what you actually control. Where are you looking? What are you reaching for? Everything in the future is uncertain. Live right now.

shortness-of-life_section-09.originalText:
See how the greatest of bards cries to you and sings in wholesome verse as though inspired with celestial fire:—

"The best of wretched mortals' days is that Which is the first to fly."

Why do you hesitate, says he, why do you stand back? unless you seize it it will have fled: and even if you do seize it, it will still fly. Our swiftness in making use of our time ought therefore to vie with the swiftness of time itself, and we ought to drink of it as we should of a fast-running torrent which will not be always running. The poet, too, admirably satirizes our boundless thoughts, when he says, not "the first age," but "the first day." Why are you careless and slow while time is flying so fast, and why do you spread out before yourself a vision of long months and years, as many as your greediness requires? he talks with you about one day, and that a fast-fleeting one.
shortness-of-life_section-09.plainEnglish:
Look at what the greatest poet tells us, singing with divine inspiration:

"The best day of our miserable lives is the one that flies away first."

Why do you hesitate? Why do you hold back? Unless you grab that day, it will escape. And even if you do grab it, it will still slip away. We need to use our time as quickly as time itself moves. We should drink from it like we're drinking from a rushing river that won't flow forever. The poet brilliantly mocks our endless planning when he says "the first day," not "the first age." Why are you lazy and slow when time races by so fast? Why do you imagine months and years stretching ahead of you — as many as your greedy heart wants? He's talking about one single day. And that day flies by quickly.

shortness-of-life_section-09.originalText: There can, then, be no doubt that the best days are those which fly first for wretched, that is, for busy mortals, whose minds are still in their childhood when old age comes upon them, and they reach it unprepared and without arms to combat it. They have never looked forward: they have all of a sudden stumbled upon old age: they never noticed that it was stealing upon them day by day. As conversation, or reading, or deep thought deceives travellers, and they find themselves at their journey's end before they knew that it was drawing near, so in this fast and never-ceasing journey of life, which we make at the same pace whether we are asleep or awake, busy people never notice that they are moving till they are at the end of it.
shortness-of-life_section-09.plainEnglish: The best days always disappear first for unhappy people — that is, for busy people. Their minds are still childish when old age hits them. They reach it unprepared and defenseless. They never looked ahead. They stumble into old age suddenly. They never noticed it creeping up on them day by day. Just like conversation or reading or deep thinking can distract travelers so they arrive at their destination before they realize they're close, busy people never notice they're moving through life's fast, never-stopping journey until they reach the end.

shortness-of-life_section-10.originalText: If I chose to divide this proposition into separate steps, supported by evidence, many things occur to me by which I could prove that the lives of busy men are the shortest of all. Fabianus, who was none of your lecture-room philosophers, but one of the true antique pattern, used to say, "We ought to fight against the passions by main force, not by skirmishing, and upset their line of battle by a home charge, not by inflicting trifling wounds: I do not approve of dallying with sophisms; they must be crushed, not merely scratched." Yet, in order that sinners may be confronted with their errors, they must be taught, and not merely mourned for.
shortness-of-life_section-10.plainEnglish: If I wanted to break this argument down step by step with proof, I could show you many ways that busy people actually have the shortest lives of all. Fabianus wasn't one of those classroom philosophers. He was from the old school — a real philosopher. He used to say, "We need to fight our emotions head-on, not dance around them. Charge straight at them and break their line. Don't just give them little cuts. I don't believe in playing word games with clever arguments. You have to crush bad habits, not just scratch at them." But if we want to help people see their mistakes, we need to teach them, not just feel sorry for them.

shortness-of-life_section-10.originalText: Life is divided into three parts: that which has been, that which is, and that which is to come: of these three stages, that which we are passing through is brief, that which we are about to pass is uncertain, and that which we have passed is certain: this it is over which Fortune has lost her rights, and which can fall into no other man's power: and this is what busy men lose: for they have no leisure to look back upon the past, and even if they had, they take no pleasure in remembering what they regret: they are, therefore, unwilling to turn their minds to the contemplation of ill-spent time, and they shrink from reviewing a course of action whose faults become glaringly apparent when handled a second time, although they were snatched at when we were under the spell of immediate gratification.
shortness-of-life_section-10.plainEnglish: Life has three parts: what has happened, what is happening now, and what will happen. The present moment is brief. The future is uncertain. But the past is certain — and it's the only part that Fortune can't touch or that no one can take from you. Yet this is exactly what busy people lose. They have no time to look back at their past. And even if they did have time, they wouldn't enjoy remembering things they regret. So they refuse to think about the time they've wasted. They shrink from reviewing their choices, because the mistakes become painfully obvious when you look back — even though those same choices seemed appealing when you were caught up in the moment.

shortness-of-life_section-10.originalText: No one, unless all his acts have been submitted to the infallible censorship of his own conscience, willingly turns his thoughts back upon the past. He who has ambitiously desired, haughtily scorned, passionately vanquished, treacherously deceived, greedily snatched, or prodigally wasted much, must needs fear his own memory; yet this is a holy and consecrated part of our time, beyond the reach of all human accidents, removed from the dominion of Fortune, and which cannot be disquieted by want, fear, or attacks of sickness: this can neither be troubled nor taken away from one: we possess it for ever undisturbed.
shortness-of-life_section-10.plainEnglish: No one likes to look back on their past unless they can honestly say their conscience is clear. If you've been driven by ambition, looked down on others with arrogance, won through passion, deceived people, grabbed things greedily, or thrown away what you had — then you're going to fear your own memories. But here's the thing: the past is actually sacred. It's the one part of our time that can't be touched by accidents, bad luck, poverty, fear, or disease. Nothing can disturb it or steal it from you. It's yours forever, completely safe.

shortness-of-life_section-10.originalText: Our present consists only of single days, and those, too, taken one hour at a time: but all the days of past times appear before us when bidden, and allow themselves to be examined and lingered over, albeit busy men cannot find time for so doing. It is the privilege of a tranquil and peaceful mind to review all the parts of its life: but the minds of busy men are like animals under the yoke, and cannot bend aside or look back. Consequently, their life passes away into vacancy, and as you do no good however much you may pour into a vessel which cannot keep or hold what you put there, so also it matters not how much time you give men if it can find no place to settle in, but leaks away through the chinks and holes of their minds.
shortness-of-life_section-10.plainEnglish: Right now, we only have today — and even that comes to us one hour at a time. But all our past days are there waiting for us when we call them up. We can examine them and linger over them — if we're not too busy to bother. Only a calm and peaceful mind can review all the parts of its life. But busy minds are like animals pulling a cart. They can't turn aside or look back. So their life just disappears into nothing. It's like pouring water into a broken bucket — no matter how much time you give people, if their minds can't hold onto it, it all leaks out through the cracks.

shortness-of-life_section-10.originalText: Present time is very short, so much so that to some it seems to be no time at all; for it is always in motion, and runs swiftly away: it ceases to exist before it comes, and can no more brook delay than can the universe or the host of heaven, whose unresting movement never lets them pause on their way. Busy men, therefore, possess present time, alone, that being so short that they cannot grasp it, and when they are occupied with many things they lose even this.
shortness-of-life_section-10.plainEnglish: The present moment is incredibly short — so short that some people feel like it doesn't exist at all. It's always moving and rushing past us. It disappears before it even arrives, and it can't be slowed down any more than you can stop the universe or the stars in their endless motion across the sky. So busy people only have this present moment to work with. But it's so brief they can't even grab hold of it. And when they're juggling too many things at once, they lose even this tiny sliver of time they have.

shortness-of-life_section-11.originalText:
In a word, do you want to know for how short a time they live?
see how they desire to live long: broken-down old men beg in their
prayers for the addition of a few more years: they pretend to be
younger than they are: they delude themselves with their own lies,
and are as willing to cheat themselves as if they could cheat Fate
at the same time: when at last some weakness reminds them that they
are mortal, they die as it were in terror: they may rather
be said to be dragged out of this life than to depart from it. They
loudly exclaim that they have been fools and have not lived their
lives, and declare that if they only survive this sickness they
will spend the rest of their lives at leisure: at such times they
reflect how uselessly they have laboured to provide themselves with
what they have never enjoyed, and how all their toil has gone for
nothing: but those whose life is spent without any engrossing
business may well find it ample: no part of it is made over to
others, or scattered here and there; no part is entrusted to Fortune,
is lost by neglect, is spent in ostentatious giving, or is useless:
all of it is, so to speak, invested at good interest. A very small
amount of it, therefore, is abundantly sufficient, and so, when his
last day arrives, the wise man will not hang back, but will walk
with a steady step to meet death.
shortness-of-life_section-11.plainEnglish: Want to know how short their lives really are? Look at how desperately they want to live longer. Old, broken-down men pray for just a few more years. They lie about their age. They fool themselves with their own lies, willing to deceive themselves as if they could somehow trick Fate too. When illness finally reminds them they're mortal, they die in terror. They're not leaving life — they're being dragged out of it kicking and screaming. They cry out that they've been fools, that they never really lived. They promise that if they survive this illness, they'll finally live at leisure. They realize how pointlessly they worked for things they never enjoyed. All their effort was wasted. But people who don't waste their lives on meaningless busy work find life plenty long. They don't hand pieces of it over to others or scatter it everywhere. They don't trust it to luck, lose it through neglect, waste it showing off, or throw it away. All of it pays good returns, you could say. Even a small amount is more than enough. So when the wise person's last day comes, he won't hold back or hesitate. He'll walk steadily toward death.

shortness-of-life_section-12.originalText: Perhaps you will ask me whom I mean by "busy men"? you need not think that I allude only to those who are hunted out of the courts of justice with dogs at the close of the proceedings, those whom you see either honourably jostled by a crowd of their own clients or contemptuously hustled in visits of ceremony by strangers, who call them away from home to hang about their patron's doors, or who make use of the praetor's sales by auction to acquire infamous gains which some day will prove their own ruin. Some men's leisure is busy: in their country house or on their couch, in complete solitude, even though they have retired from all men's society, they still continue to worry themselves: we ought not to say that such men's life is one of leisure, but their very business is sloth.
shortness-of-life_section-12.plainEnglish: Maybe you're wondering what I mean by "busy men." I'm not just talking about lawyers who get chased out of courtrooms when court ends, or those you see either proudly surrounded by their own clients or rudely pushed around by strangers during formal visits. I don't just mean the ones who drag them away from home to wait around at their patron's door, or who use the praetor's auctions to make shameful profits that will eventually destroy them. Some people are busy even in their leisure time. At their country house or lying on their couch, completely alone, even when they've withdrawn from all society, they still keep worrying themselves sick. We shouldn't call this kind of life leisurely — their business is actually laziness.

shortness-of-life_section-12.originalText: Would you call a man idle who expends anxious finicking care in the arrangement of his Corinthian bronzes, valuable only through the mania of a few connoisseurs? and who passes the greater part of his days among plates of rusty metal? who sits in the palaestra (shame, that our very vices should be foreign) watching boys wrestling? who distributes his gangs of fettered slaves into pairs according to their age and colour? who keeps athletes of the latest fashion?
shortness-of-life_section-12.plainEnglish: Would you call a man idle who spends anxious hours arranging his collection of Corinthian bronze statues — valuable only because a few collectors have gone crazy for them? A man who spends most of his days among plates of rusty metal? Who sits in the gymnasium (how shameful that even our vices come from abroad) watching boys wrestle? Who sorts his chained slaves into matching pairs by age and skin color? Who keeps fashionable athletes on his payroll?

shortness-of-life_section-12.originalText: Why, do you call those men idle, who pass many hours at the barber's while the growth of the past night is being plucked out by the roots, holding councils over each several hair, while the scattered locks are arranged in order and those which fall back are forced forward on to the forehead? How angry they become if the shaver is a little careless, as though he were shearing a _man_! what a white heat they work themselves into if some of their mane is cut away, if some part of it is ill-arranged, if all their ringlets do not lie in regular order! who of them would not rather that the state were overthrown than that his hair should be ruffled? who does not care more for the appearance of his head than for his health? who would not prefer ornament to honour?
shortness-of-life_section-12.plainEnglish: Do you really think those men are idle who spend hours at the barber? They sit there while last night's stubble gets plucked out by the roots. They hold meetings about every single hair. They arrange scattered locks just so, forcing back hair forward onto their foreheads. How furious they get if the barber slips up a little — as if he were cutting a real man! They work themselves into a rage if any of their precious mane gets trimmed wrong. If some part doesn't sit right. If all their curls don't lie in perfect rows. Which of them wouldn't rather see the government collapse than have his hair messed up? Which one doesn't care more about how his head looks than his actual health? Which one wouldn't choose decoration over honor?

shortness-of-life_section-12.originalText: Do you call these men idle, who make a business of the comb and looking-glass? what of those who devote their lives to composing, hearing, and learning songs, who twist their voices, intended by Nature to sound best and simplest when used straightforwardly, through all the turns of futile melodies: whose fingers are always beating time to some music on which they are inwardly meditating; who, when invited to serious and even sad business may be heard humming an air to themselves?—such people are not at leisure, but are busy about trifles.
shortness-of-life_section-12.plainEnglish: Do you think these men are idle — the ones who spend all their time fussing with their hair and mirrors? What about those who devote their entire lives to writing songs, listening to music, and learning new tunes? They twist their voices through pointless melodies when nature meant them to sound best when used simply and directly. Their fingers are always tapping out rhythms to whatever music is playing in their heads. Even when they're called to handle serious or sad business, you can hear them humming to themselves. These people aren't relaxing — they're just busy with nonsense.

shortness-of-life_section-12.originalText: As for their banquets, by Hercules, I cannot reckon them among their unoccupied times when I see with what anxious care they set out their plate, how laboriously they arrange the girdles of their waiters' tunics, how breathlessly they watch to see how the cook dishes up the wild boar, with what speed, when the signal is given, the slave-boys run to perform their duties, how skilfully birds are carved into pieces of the right size, how painstakingly wretched youths wipe up the spittings of drunken men. By these means men seek credit for taste and grandeur, and their vices follow them so far into their privacy that they can neither eat nor drink without a view to effect.
shortness-of-life_section-12.plainEnglish: As for their fancy dinner parties — good God, I can't count these as free time when I see how anxiously they arrange their silverware. They fuss over how their servants' clothes are arranged. They watch with bated breath to see how the cook presents the roasted boar. When the signal comes, slave boys rush around doing their jobs. Birds must be carved into perfect pieces. Poor young servants carefully clean up the spit from drunk guests. Through all this, the hosts are trying to look refined and impressive. Their need to show off follows them everywhere — they can't even eat or drink without putting on a performance.

shortness-of-life_section-12.originalText: Nor should I count those men idle who have themselves carried hither and thither in sedans and litters, and who look forward to their regular hour for taking this exercise as though they were not allowed to omit it: men who are reminded by some one else when to bathe, when to swim, when to dine: they actually reach such a pitch of languid effeminacy as not to be able to find out for themselves whether they are hungry.
shortness-of-life_section-12.plainEnglish: I also wouldn't call those men idle who get carried around in chairs and litters, and who wait for their scheduled exercise time as if they're not allowed to skip it. These are men who need someone else to tell them when to bathe, when to swim, when to eat. They've become so soft and weak that they can't even figure out for themselves whether they're hungry.

shortness-of-life_section-12.originalText: I have heard one of these luxurious folk—if indeed, we ought to give the name of luxury to unlearning the life and habits of a man—when he was carried in men's arms out of the bath and placed in his chair, say inquiringly, "Am I seated?" Do you suppose that such a man as this, who did not know when he was seated, could know whether he was alive, whether he could see, whether he was at leisure? I can hardly say whether I pity him more if he really did not know or if he pretended not to know this. Such people do really become unconscious of much, but they behave as though they were unconscious of much more: they delight in some failings because they consider them to be proofs of happiness: it seems the part of an utterly low and contemptible man to know what he is doing.
shortness-of-life_section-12.plainEnglish: I once heard one of these pampered rich people—though we shouldn't really call it luxury when someone has forgotten how to be human—being carried from his bath and placed in his chair. He asked, 'Am I sitting down?' Can you believe it? A man who doesn't know if he's sitting—how could he know if he's alive? Or if he can see? Or if he has any free time? I honestly can't tell what's worse: if he really didn't know, or if he was just pretending. These people genuinely lose awareness of many things. But they also act like they're unaware of even more. They enjoy some of these failings because they think it proves how wealthy they are. Apparently, only poor, worthless people need to know what they're doing.

shortness-of-life_section-12.originalText: After this, do you suppose that playwrights draw largely upon their imaginations in their burlesques upon luxury: by Hercules, they omit more than they invent; in this age, inventive in this alone, such a number of incredible vices have been produced, that already you are able to reproach the playwrights with omitting to notice them. To think that there should be any one who had so far lost his senses through luxury as to take some one else's opinion as to whether he was sitting or not? This man certainly is not at leisure: you must bestow a different title on him: he is sick, or rather dead: he only is at leisure who feels that he is at leisure: but this creature is only half alive, if he wants some one to tell him what position his body is in. How can such a man be able to dispose of any time?
shortness-of-life_section-12.plainEnglish: After hearing all this, do you think playwrights have to stretch their imaginations when they make fun of luxury in their comedies? By God, they leave out more than they make up. In our age — which seems to excel only at inventing new vices — so many unbelievable forms of corruption have appeared that you could actually criticize playwrights for not noticing them all. Can you imagine someone so ruined by luxury that he needs another person to tell him whether he's sitting down or not? This man is definitely not living a life of leisure. You need a different word for him: he's sick, or really he's dead. Only someone who knows he's at leisure is truly at leisure. But this poor creature is only half alive if he needs someone else to tell him what position his body is in. How could such a person possibly have control over his time?

shortness-of-life_section-13.originalText: It would take long to describe the various individuals who have wasted their lives over playing at draughts, playing at ball, or toasting their bodies in the sun: men are not at leisure if their pleasures partake of the character of business, for no one will doubt that those persons are laborious triflers who devote themselves to the study of futile literary questions, of whom there is already a great number in Rome also. It used to be a peculiarly Greek disease of the mind to investigate how many rowers Ulysses had, whether the Iliad or the Odyssey was written first, and furthermore, whether they were written by the same author, with other matters of the same stamp, which neither please your inner consciousness if you keep them to yourself, nor make you seem more learned, but only more troublesome, if you publish them abroad.
shortness-of-life_section-13.plainEnglish: It would take forever to list all the people who waste their lives playing board games, sports, or lying in the sun. These people aren't really at leisure if their fun feels like work. And no one would argue that people who spend their time on pointless academic questions are anything but busy fools. We already have too many of these in Rome. This used to be a uniquely Greek mental disease — debating how many rowers Ulysses had, whether the Iliad or Odyssey was written first, whether the same person wrote both, and other equally useless questions. These debates won't satisfy you if you keep them private, and they won't make you seem smarter if you share them — just more annoying.

shortness-of-life_section-13.originalText: See, already this vain longing to learn what is useless has taken hold of the Romans: the other day I heard somebody telling who was the first Roman general who did this or that: Duillius was the first who won a sea-fight, Curius Dentatus was the first who drove elephants in his triumph: moreover, these stories, though they add nothing to real glory, do nevertheless deal with the great deeds of our countrymen: such knowledge is not profitable, yet it claims our attention as a fascinating kind of folly. I will even pardon those who want to know who first persuaded the Romans to go on board ship. It was Claudius, who for this reason was surnamed Caudex, because any piece of carpentry formed of many planks was called _caudex_ by the ancient Romans, for which reason public records are called _Codices_, and by old custom the ships which ply on the Tiber with provisions are called _codicariae_.
shortness-of-life_section-13.plainEnglish: Look, this pointless urge to learn useless facts has already infected the Romans. Just the other day I heard someone explaining who was the first Roman general to do this or that. Duillius was the first to win a sea battle. Curius Dentatus was the first to parade elephants in his victory march. Now, these stories don't add anything to real glory, but at least they deal with our countrymen's great deeds. This kind of knowledge isn't useful, yet it grabs our attention like an entertaining bit of foolishness. I'll even forgive people who want to know who first convinced the Romans to get on ships. It was Claudius, who got the nickname Caudex because the ancient Romans called any wooden structure made of many planks a caudex. That's why public records are called Codices, and why the supply ships that travel the Tiber are still called codicariae.

shortness-of-life_section-13.originalText: Let us also allow that it is to the point to tell how Valerius Corvinus was the first to conquer Messana, and first of the family of the Valerii transferred the name of the captured city to his own, and was called Messana, and how the people gradually corrupted the pronunciation and called him Messalla: or would you let any one find interest in Lucius Sulla having been the first to let lions loose in the circus, they having been previously exhibited in chains, and hurlers of darts having been sent by King Bocchus to kill them? This may be permitted to their curiosity: but can it serve any useful purpose to know that Pompeius was the first to exhibit eighteen elephants in the circus, who were matched in a mimic battle with some convicts? The leading man in the state, and one who, according to tradition, was noted among the ancient leaders of the state for his transcendent goodness of heart, thought it a notable kind of show to kill men in a manner hitherto unheard of.
shortness-of-life_section-13.plainEnglish: Let's say it's worth knowing that Valerius Corvinus was the first to conquer Messana. He took the city's name for himself and became known as Messana. Over time, people changed how they said it and called him Messalla. Or maybe you'd find it interesting that Lucius Sulla was the first to release lions in the circus — before him, they were only shown in chains. King Bocchus sent dart-throwers to kill them. Fine, let people be curious about these things. But what's the point of knowing that Pompey was the first to put eighteen elephants in the circus and made them fight condemned criminals? Here was Rome's leading citizen — a man famous among our ancestors for his exceptional kindness — and he thought it was entertaining to kill people in a completely new way.

shortness-of-life_section-13.originalText: Do they fight to the death? that is not cruel enough: are they torn to pieces? that is not cruel enough: let them be crushed flat by animals of enormous bulk. It would be much better that such a thing should be forgotten, for fear that hereafter some potentate might hear of it and envy its refined barbarity. O, how doth excessive prosperity blind our intellects! at the moment at which he was casting so many troops of wretches to be trampled on by outlandish beasts, when he was proclaiming war between such different creatures, when he was shedding so much blood before the eyes of the Roman people, whose blood he himself was soon to shed even more freely, he thought himself the master of the whole world; yet he afterwards, deceived by the treachery of the Alexandrians, had to offer himself to the dagger of the vilest of slaves, and then at last discovered what an empty boast was his surname of "The Great."
shortness-of-life_section-13.plainEnglish: Do they fight to the death? That's not cruel enough. Are they torn apart? Still not cruel enough. Let them be crushed by massive animals. It would be better if such things were forgotten entirely — otherwise some future ruler might hear about it and try to copy this refined savagery. Oh, how too much power blinds us! At the very moment he was throwing crowds of poor souls to be trampled by exotic beasts, when he was staging battles between completely different creatures, when he was spilling so much blood in front of the Roman people (whose blood he would soon spill even more freely), he thought he ruled the entire world. But later, fooled by treacherous Alexandrians, he had to offer himself to the blade of the lowest slave. Only then did he discover how empty his nickname "The Great" really was.

shortness-of-life_section-13.originalText: But to return to the point from which I have digressed, I will prove that even on this very subject some people expend useless pains. The same author tells us that Metellus, when he triumphed after having conquered the Carthaginians in Sicily, was the only Roman who ever had a hundred and twenty captured elephants led before his car: and that Sulla was the last Roman who extended the pomoerium,[7] which it was not the custom of the ancients to extend on account of the conquest of provincial, but only of Italian territory. Is it more useful to know this, than to know that the Mount Aventine, according to him, is outside of the pomoerium, for one of two reasons, either because it was thither that the plebeians seceded, or because when Remus took his auspices on that place the birds which he saw were not propitious: and other stories without number of the like sort, which are either actual falsehoods or much the same as falsehoods? for even if you allow that these authors speak in all good faith, if they pledge themselves for the truth of what they write, still, whose mistakes will be made fewer by such stories? whose passions will be restrained? whom will they make more brave, more just, or more gentlemanly? My friend Fabianus used to say that he was not sure that it was not better not to apply oneself to any studies at all than to become interested in these.
shortness-of-life_section-13.plainEnglish: But let me get back to my point. I'll prove that people waste effort on useless things. The same historian tells us that Metellus was the only Roman to have 120 captured elephants parade in front of his chariot after defeating the Carthaginians in Sicily. He also says Sulla was the last Roman to extend the pomoerium — something the ancients only did for conquering Italian territory, not foreign provinces. Is it more useful to know this than to know why Mount Aventine sits outside the pomoerium? Maybe because the plebeians fled there once, or because when Remus took his bird omens there, the signs were bad. There are countless other stories like this — either outright lies or close enough to lies. Even if you trust these authors completely, even if they guarantee everything they write is true, who becomes wiser from such stories? Who learns to control their emotions better? Who becomes braver, more just, or more noble? My friend Fabianus used to say he wasn't sure it wouldn't be better to avoid all studies rather than get caught up in this nonsense.

shortness-of-life_section-14.originalText: The only persons who are really at leisure are those who devote themselves to philosophy: and they alone really live: for they do not merely enjoy their own lifetime, but they annex every century to their own: all the years which have passed before them belong to them.
